What the tide leaves behind

by Marin Okafor

A rock pool is a rehearsal for the whole ocean. Twice a day the water withdraws and leaves a bowl of it stranded on the shore, and for six hours everything living in that bowl has to manage without the sea. The temperature climbs. The salt concentrates. The oxygen thins out. Nothing about it is comfortable, and yet the pools are the most crowded places on the coast.

Dr. Aleen Vasquez has spent eleven seasons counting the animals in a single stretch of granite shelf. Her argument is that the crowding is not despite the hardship but because of it. A creature that can survive six hours of a hot, salty, airless bowl can survive almost anything else the shore throws at it, and in exchange it gets a address that larger predators cannot reach at low water.

Measuring a pool

The standard method is a quadrat: a square frame laid on the rock, with everything inside it identified and counted. It sounds crude and it is, but it has the advantage of being repeatable by anyone, which is why the records go back to the 1930s in some places.

What the long records show is not a steady picture. Populations in the pools swing hard from year to year, far harder than populations in the open subtidal zone a few metres away. See Fig. 4 for the clearest example, a twenty-year run of limpet counts that looks more like weather than biology.

A rough model

The simplest model that reproduces the swings treats each pool as a small island, repopulated every season from a shared larval pool. Something like this:

def settle(pool, larvae, carrying_capacity):
    arrivals = larvae * pool.exposure
    survivors = min(arrivals, carrying_capacity - pool.occupied)
    pool.occupied += max(survivors, 0)
    return pool

It is far too simple to predict anything. What it does do is show that you get wild swings without needing to invent a cause for them: random arrival into a small space is enough on its own, which is a useful thing to know before you start looking for a pollutant.

What to look at

  • Start at the lowest pool you can reach safely and work upward, because the lower pools are richer and will calibrate your eye for the sparse ones.
  • Look under the ledges rather than at the open floor, since almost everything mobile is hiding from the light and the gulls.
  • Go back to the same pool. One visit tells you almost nothing at all.

The last point is the one people skip. A single visit to a rock pool is a photograph of a room taken through a keyhole, and the whole interest of the place is in how violently it changes between one visit and the next.
